newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto's real estate market heating up.
newsitem.headline: Toronto's real estate market heating up.

text.p: Stewart and Dianne Hall had high aspirations when they listed their three-bedroom bungalow for C$264,900 in Canada's largest city.
But even Mr. Hall was shocked when their "very average house" fetched C$15,000 over the asking price in a frenzied nine-party bidding war.
"It was completely unexpected, like winning the lottery," Mr. Hall said.

The Halls are not alone. In a trend reminiscent of the late 1980's real estate boom in Toronto, multiple buyers are again competing for Toronto's houses and bidding up prices. According to The Toronto Star, one house recently sold for a record breaking $83,000 above its stated listing.
Indicative of good economic times to come, Toronto's housing boom may place it in the lead of Canada's economic growth.

"The boom here is very strong, largely reflecting growth in Toronto," according to Will Dunning, Senior Market Analyst at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. The surplus of confident first time buyers and upscalers promises to cause a spin off in the creation of 10,000 construction jobs in the next year, he said.
Alex Mills, of Prudential Sadie Moranis Realty, the Hall's agent, attributed the recent trend to a market that has more buyers than inventory, especially under the C$300,000 range.
"Many of them are first time buyers who are feeling more confident that they will keep at least one of their jobs and are worried that interest rates will go up," he said.

According to the Toronto Real Estate Board's Multiple Listings Service (MLS), February marked a 27 percent increase in sales over January 1997. It was also a 24 percent increase from February last year.
The average price of a single family house rose to C$207,221 in February from C$192,406 last year. Ten years ago, MLS reported the average selling price was C$124,301.
The combination of pent up demand and a feeling of improved confidence has led to a buoyancy in the market," explained analyst Barry Lyon of Lyon Consultants Ltd.

He added that the recent rise in housing sales indicated a positive trend that will continue with moderately priced homes over next several years. "People are feeling better about the economy which comes at a good time because their housing needs are changing."

Investors outside the greater Toronto area are also cashing in on its recent good rates. Many American, German and even Canadian investors outside of Ontario, such as British Columbia, consider real estate in Toronto a sound investment opportuniy since the market has yet to peak. The same applies for the industrial and commercial market.

Yet, Toronto's new case of contagious optimism leads some analysts to worry about a crash if the market gets too heated. Although speculation has not distorted the market yet -- as it did in 1986-88 in Toronto -- a dramatic rise in costs will turn off potential buyers, killing the market.
Lyon suggested remaining calm: "I feel like a fire marshal. There is a shortage of listings and it is an excellent time for people to sell their home. But if you don't like a price, just pass."

Some agents, for the time being, remained skeptical of the boom's longevity. "I wouldn't call it a boom, exactly" said Rosaline Kennanni, an agent at Coldwell, Banker & Pinnacle. "The recipe is there. Mortgage rates are low, people are finding it more economical to buy than rent. But who can tell how long it will last?"
